objective: By the end of this lesson you can run the before-takeoff check in a complex or technically advanced airplane to commercial standards: position the airplane well, test the engine, propeller, systems and avionics, explain why each item matters, and brief a takeoff with clear abort and engine-failure plans.
why: About one in five yearly GA accidents happen during takeoff and departure climb, and more than half of those are pilot failures [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. The run-up and the briefing are where you catch a sick engine, a wrong runway or a wake hazard while you are still safely on the ground.

warmup: The run-up pad is crowded, so you skip the prop cycle in your constant-speed prop airplane on a cold morning. What could happen when you push the throttle up for takeoff?

key_terms.def: The systematic AFM/POH check of engine, controls, systems, instruments and avionics before flight [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].
A controllable-pitch prop whose governor changes blade angle to hold the rpm you select [[1:166|PHAK 7-6]].
Uses engine oil pressure to change blade angle and hold the selected rpm [[24:238|AFH 12-7]].
Absolute pressure in the intake manifold; with a constant-speed prop it shows engine power [[1:166|PHAK 7-6]].
Full authority digital engine control: a computer runs engine and prop; no magnetos, carb heat or mixture lever [[1:180|PHAK 7-20]].
Stopping a takeoff on the runway for a powerplant problem, poor acceleration, incursion or traffic conflict [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].
Best angle of climb: most altitude gain in a given distance, used to clear obstacles [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].
Best rate of climb: most altitude gain in the least time [[24:375|AFH G-3]].
Any runway event with an aircraft, vehicle, person or object that creates a collision hazard or loss of separation [[1:365|PHAK 14-31]].
ATC instruction to enter the runway and hold in position; it is not a takeoff clearance [[1:368|PHAK 14-34]].
Two counter-rotating vortices trailing any aircraft that is making lift [[34:147|AIM 7-4-1]].

chunks.title: The before-takeoff check at commercial level

body.p: The before-takeoff check is the systematic AFM/POH procedure for checking the engine, controls, systems, instruments and avionics before flight [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]. Every airplane has different equipment, so you use that airplane's own AFM/POH checklist [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].
As a private pilot you learned the flow. At commercial level the examiner also wants the reason for each item, what a failure would look like, and what you will do about it (ACS CA.II.F.K1).

callout.text: Commercial training includes 10 hours in a complex airplane, a turbine-powered airplane or a technically advanced airplane (TAA) [[60:314|14 CFR 61.129(a)(3)(ii)]]. A complex airplane has retractable gear, flaps, and either a controllable-pitch prop or a FADEC engine control [[60:184|14 CFR 61.1]]. Expect prop, cowl flap and glass-panel items your trainer never had.

head: For each item, be ready to say
Example: oil temperature
rows: Why you check it (K1a)
Many engines need a minimum oil temperature before takeoff power [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]
What a malfunction looks like (K1b)
Still below the AFM/POH minimum at the run-up spot [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]
What the manufacturer says is safe (K1c)
The AFM/POH value, not a rule of thumb [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]

callout.text: If a handbook and your AFM/POH differ, the manufacturer's recommendations take precedence [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. Finish all run-up and pre-takeoff items before you taxi onto the runway [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

check.q: The AFH and your POH describe the run-up differently. Which do you follow?
check.a: The AFM/POH. The manufacturer's recommendations take precedence [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

chunks.title: Position the airplane: wind, prop blast and debris

body.p: Normally you do the check at a run-up spot near the takeoff end of the runway [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]. Where you park matters as much as what you check.

head: Do this
Why
rows: Pick a firm spot (paved or smooth turf) free of debris
The prop picks up pebbles, dirt or sand and throws them back. Chips in the blade become stress risers that can crack it, and the tail can be hit too [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]
Stay clear of other aircraft and the taxiway
So you don't block or hit anyone [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]
Check that nothing is behind you
Prop blast can damage and upset aircraft, vehicles and equipment at close range [[24:58|AFH 2-21]] [[33:262|AIM 4-3-18e]]
Point the nose as nearly into the wind as you can
Air-cooled engines get little cooling air on the ground. Cylinders can overheat before oil temperature rises [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]
Roll forward a little, then stop
Lines the nosewheel or tailwheel up with the airplane [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]
Cowl flaps as the AFM/POH says (normally open on the ground)
Ground running needs all the cooling you can get [[24:54|AFH 2-17]] [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]

body.p: Pilots call harm from loose objects foreign object damage (FOD). The PHAK describes it for turbine inlets that swallow small objects from the ramp, taxiway or runway [[1:183|PHAK 7-23]]. Your prop takes the same kind of nicks from the same debris [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

callout.text: Prop and jet blast from large aircraft has overturned or damaged smaller aircraft taxiing behind them. A lit rotating beacon is a hint that engines are running, but don't rely on it alone [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24d]].
Firm, Free of debris, Clear behind, Into the wind, Nose straight.

check.q: Why point the nose into the wind for the run-up?
check.a: To cut cylinder overheating. On the ground little cooling air goes through the cowling, and cylinders can overheat before oil temperature shows it [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

chunks.title: Engine checks: magnetos, carb heat and mixture

body.p: Each of the two magnetos fires one of the two spark plugs in every cylinder, so if one fails the other keeps the engine running [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]]. At run-up power, move the switch from BOTH to RIGHT, back to BOTH, then to LEFT, and watch the rpm decrease. A small drop is normal; the allowed drop is in the AFM/POH [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]].

head: You see
It means
Action
rows: Small drop, within POH limits
Normal [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]]
Continue
Drop over the limit, or the engine stops on one mag
Fouled plugs, broken or shorted wires, or bad timing [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]] [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]
Don't fly until it is fixed
No drop at all
Not normal [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]
Don't fly

body.p: A FADEC engine has no magnetos, carb heat or mixture lever [[1:180|PHAK 7-20]]. You still confirm that single or dual ignition operation is acceptable and within limits, the way the AFM/POH says [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].
Check carburetor heat during the run-up [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]. Heated air is less dense, so power drops, sometimes up to 15 percent [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]. What you watch depends on the propeller:

head: Propeller
Carb heat ON, no ice
Carb heat ON, ice present
rows: Fixed pitch
rpm drops, then stays constant [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]
rpm drops, then slowly rises as the ice melts [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]
Constant speed
MP drops; no gradual rise until heat is off [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]
MP drops, then gradually rises [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]

callout.text: With a constant-speed prop, carb ice shows as lower manifold pressure with no rpm change, because the governor changes pitch to hold rpm [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]. Watch the MP gauge, not the tach.

body.p: At high-elevation airports a full-rich mixture can foul the plugs during the run-up [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]]. One POH example says to lean for maximum rpm in a full-throttle static run-up before takeoff from fields above 3,000 feet [[1:278|PHAK Figure 11-24]]. Use your own POH procedure.

check.q: Constant-speed prop, carb heat ON at run-up. Which gauge tells you ice was there, and how?
check.a: Manifold pressure. It drops and then gradually rises as the ice melts. rpm stays put because the governor holds it [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

chunks.title: Constant-speed prop: cycle it and read it

body.p: A constant-speed prop has two controls. The throttle controls power, which shows on the manifold pressure gauge. The prop control sets rpm, which shows on the tachometer. A governor then changes blade angle to hold that rpm [[1:166|PHAK 7-6]].

With the engine off, the MP gauge shows ambient air pressure (for example 29.92 "Hg). After start it drops, for example to about 12 "Hg at idle. The green arc is the normal range and the red radial line is the upper limit [[1:166|PHAK 7-6]].

The governor uses engine oil pressure to change blade angle [[24:238|AFH 12-7]]. Oil has sat in the prop cylinder since the last shutdown. Some leaks out, and the rest tends to congeal, especially when it is cold [[24:239|AFH 12-8]].

head: Prop cycle step
What you look for
rows: Prop control full forward (low pitch, high rpm) for start and warm-up
Less prop load, so easier starting and warm-up [[24:239|AFH 12-8]]
Set MP for about 1,600 rpm (or the POH value)
Enough power for a clear check [[24:239|AFH 12-8]]
Move the prop control slowly and smoothly to high pitch, low rpm
rpm comes down and stabilizes [[24:239|AFH 12-8]]
Move it back to the low pitch, takeoff position
rpm returns and the engine keeps running normally [[24:239|AFH 12-8]] [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]

body.p: This proves the system works and circulates fresh, warm oil through the governor. Skip it and the engine may overspeed on takeoff [[24:239|AFH 12-8]].

callout.text: On the takeoff roll, the tach should come up to within 40 rpm of the red line as soon as you apply full power, and stay there [[24:239|AFH 12-8]]. Anything else is a powerplant malfunction, a reason to reject the takeoff [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].
More power: rpm up first, then MP. Less power: MP down first, then rpm [[24:239|AFH 12-8]].

check.q: Give the two reasons for cycling a constant-speed prop during the run-up.
check.a: To prove the system works, and to circulate fresh warm oil through the governor so the engine doesn't overspeed on takeoff [[24:239|AFH 12-8]].

head: Gauge
What it tells you
Trouble sign
rows: Ammeter
Plus side: the battery is charging [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]
Full-scale minus: alternator/generator problem. Full-scale plus: regulator problem [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]
Loadmeter
Load on the alternator, starting at zero. With everything off, only the battery's charging current [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]
Use the AFM/POH for abnormal readings
Voltage
Should be in range with the battery charging [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]
Alternator output should be above battery voltage, about 14 volts for a 12-volt battery [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]
Suction
Typically 4.8 to 5.2 "Hg at 2,000 rpm; use POH values [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]
Gyros may not spin up or read right [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]
Oil pressure
Green arc is normal [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]
Red marks the minimum and maximum [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]
Oil temp and CHT
Oil at least the POH minimum before high power [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]
Cylinders can overheat on the ground before oil temperature rises [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]

body.p: Some airplanes have a warning light instead of an ammeter. When it is on, the generator or alternator is not charging [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]].

callout.text: Mechanical gyros need time to spool up. A hasty taxi and run-up followed by a departure into IMC is unadvisable [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

check.q: Your 12-volt airplane shows about 12 volts at run-up rpm. Is the alternator charging?
check.a: Probably not. Alternator output should be higher than battery voltage, about 14 volts for a 12-volt battery. Check the AFM/POH [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]].

chunks.title: Controls, trim, instruments, avionics and autopilot

body.p: Flight controls: move aileron, elevator and rudder to full deflection in all directions. Pilots often don't use the full range, and that is not acceptable [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]. Check for full, free and correct movement [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].
Trim: set for takeoff. That is elevator trim, plus rudder and aileron trim if you have them [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

Flight instruments: the heading indicator agrees with the magnetic compass, and the heading bug is on the runway heading or the heading ATC gave you [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]. Set to the current altimeter setting, the altimeter should read field elevation within 75 feet for IFR flight [[24:42|AFH 2-5]].
Avionics: set frequencies, the first navigation source and course, autopilot preselects, transponder code and other settings for your equipment and flight [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

Glass-panel airplanes have their own checks: red Xs should clear from engine and flight displays as sensors come on line, pitot-static and attitude displays work, alarms and annunciators test, fuel levels are set and avionics cooling fans run. The AFM/POH says how [[24:42|AFH 2-5]] [[24:43|AFH 2-6]].

callout.text: Autopilot: the AFH's general advice for flight director/autopilot systems is to do all the system's computer and trim checks before you engage it. Many newer systems need a self-test first. Know the normal and emergency ways to disengage; details are in the AFM/POH supplements [[24:257|AFH 13-8]]. Autopilots have a disconnect safety feature and can be overridden by hand [[1:160|PHAK 6-12]].

body.p: Electric trim: run the trim switch nose-up and nose-down, check that the trim disconnect (if installed) works, then set takeoff trim [[24:344|AFH 17-10]]. Runaway trim is one of the mechanical failures that can upset an airplane [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. Know where the trim disconnect and the trim circuit breaker are, so you can use them quickly [[24:348|AFH 17-14]].

check.q: Set to the current altimeter setting, your altimeter reads 110 feet above field elevation. OK for an IFR departure?
check.a: No. It should read field elevation within 75 feet for IFR [[24:42|AFH 2-5]].

body.p: Always read your own AFM/POH checklist. A typical flow for a complex or TAA single looks like this [[24:58|AFH 2-21]] [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]:

head: Step
Check
rows: Position
Firm, clear spot, into the wind, nothing behind, nose straight [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]
Brakes and eyes
Brakes set; one item inside, one look outside [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]
Fuel
ON and the correct tank selected [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]
Controls and trim
Full, free and correct; trim set for takeoff [[24:58|AFH 2-21]] [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]
Temperatures
Oil at least the minimum; watch CHT; cowl flaps per POH [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]
Run-up
Mags (or FADEC test), carb heat if equipped, prop cycle [[24:58|AFH 2-21]] [[24:239|AFH 12-8]]
Electrical and vacuum
Volts in range, battery charging, suction normal [[24:58|AFH 2-21]] [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]
Instruments and avionics
Heading indicator vs compass, bug, frequencies, nav, autopilot preselects, transponder [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]
Takeoff briefing
Out loud, even alone; verify the correct runway and direction [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]
Before the runway
Scan the approach areas for landing traffic [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15a]]

body.p: As you bring in full power, run the takeoff checks: runway numbers agree with the compass and heading indicator; doors latched; controls set for crosswind; power, rpm and smoothness normal; engine instruments in the green [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].
The ACS Skills for this Task have no number tolerances. This is what the examiner grades:

head: ACS standard
What it looks like
rows: CA.II.F.S1: Review takeoff performance.
You know today's distance, the runway available, your abort point and climb speeds
CA.II.F.S2: Complete the appropriate checklist(s).
POH checklist read and done item by item
CA.II.F.S3: Position the airplane appropriately considering wind direction and the presence of any aircraft, vessels, or buildings as applicable.
Firm, clear, into the wind, nothing behind
CA.II.F.S4: Divide attention inside and outside the flight deck.
Regular looks outside; nothing creeps or surprises you
CA.II.F.S5: Verify that engine parameters and airplane configuration are suitable.
Every reading inside POH limits; trim, flaps, fuel, prop and cowl flaps set for takeoff

check.q: Before you start the takeoff roll, what must the runway numbers agree with?
check.a: The magnetic compass and the heading indicator [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

chunks.title: Review takeoff performance and brief the takeoff

body.p: Before every flight you must know the runway lengths and the AFM takeoff and landing distance data [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]]. Use the POH charts to decide if the airplane can safely take off and climb here, today. High density altitude means a longer roll and a weaker climb [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

head: Factor
Effect on takeoff distance
rows: 10 percent more weight
At least 21 percent longer [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]
Headwind 10 percent of takeoff speed
About 19 percent shorter [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]
Tailwind 10 percent of takeoff speed
About 21 percent longer [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]
Headwind 50 percent of takeoff speed
About 25 percent of the zero-wind distance [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]]
Any surface not hard and smooth
Longer ground roll [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]

body.p: Know your speeds from the POH. VR is where you rotate. VX gives the most altitude in a given distance, so use it to clear obstacles. VY gives the most altitude in a given time and is typical for a departure with no obstacles [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]. VR comes from the AFM/POH and goes in your briefing [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

Pick a point on the runway where you should be airborne. If you reach it and are not flying, stop right away. The POH takeoff and landing ground rolls added together give a good estimate of the runway you need to speed up and then stop [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

bullets: Abort criteria the AFH names: malfunctioning powerplant, inadequate acceleration, runway incursion, air traffic conflict [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].
Add your own: tach not within 40 rpm of red line at full power [[24:239|AFH 12-8]], engine instruments not in the green [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

callout.text: Sample briefing, out loud even when alone: "Normal takeoff, Runway 27, wind 250 at 8, rotate at (VR), climb at VY, runway heading to 2,000. Engine failure below VR: reject, brake, stop straight ahead. After VR with runway left: lower pitch, land, stop straight ahead. No runway left: best glide, no turns before (altitude), land in the best area. Turn back only above (AGL), which is (MSL). If time permits, fuel, ignition and electrical off." [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]

check.q: POH ground roll is 1,250 feet for takeoff and 750 feet for landing. About how much runway do you need to accelerate and stop?
check.a: About 2,000 feet: add the two ground rolls [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

body.p: Before every takeoff, think through the options if the engine fails: the preferred direction for emergency turns based on the departure path, altitude, wind and terrain [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

head: When it fails
What to do
rows: On the runway
Power to idle, maximum braking, keep it straight. For a fire, mixture to idle cutoff and mags off. Follow the POH [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]
Initial climb
Lower the nose at once: at a climb attitude with no power you are at or near the stall. Use rudder to stay coordinated and glide to a landing area, preferably straight ahead [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]
Thinking of a turn back
Only if trained in that make and model and sure you can reach the field [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]

body.p: The FAA example: engine fails at 300 feet AGL. After a 4-second reaction, a standard-rate turn through 225 degrees takes 75 more seconds. Descending about 1,000 fpm, the airplane loses 1,316 feet and ends up 1,016 feet below the runway [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]. A standard-rate or shallow turn takes too much time and distance, so a turn back needs a steeper bank [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

The R4 factors decide your plan. Airplane: some can't glide back at all [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]. Runway and takeoff path: how much is left and what lies past the end. Surface: anything not hard and smooth adds roll [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]. Environment: high density altitude cuts climb [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. Obstructions: plan VX to clear them [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].

callout.text: A low-altitude turn back is an unacceptable risk for low-time, untrained or unproficient pilots, and in airplanes without enough glide performance [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Straight ahead or a slight turn is usually the lowest-risk choice [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

check.q: In the FAA turn-back example, why does the airplane end up below the runway?
check.a: The reaction time plus a standard-rate turn through 225 degrees takes 79 seconds. At about 1,000 fpm that is 1,316 feet, more than the 300 feet it had [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

chunks.title: Divide your attention inside and outside

body.p: During the run-up, split your attention between the inside and the outside. If the parking brake slips or your toe brakes are not enough for the power, the airplane can move forward fast and go unnoticed. Use one item inside, then one look outside [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

bullets: Do pre-departure checklists only when stopped, or when taxiing straight ahead with no complex intersections [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(a)]].
Do heads-down work, like programming the GPS or working takeoff data, before taxi or while stopped [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(2)]] [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(4)]].
Ask passengers for a sterile cockpit, no unneeded talk during taxi and departure, but ask them to speak up if they see a conflict [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(b)]] [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7c]].
Phones and other devices off during taxi [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(j)]].
Approaching the runway, stop completely before going on with checklists [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(5)]].

body.p: Interruptions are a big source of error. The classic case: you put the checklist down, handle the interruption, then pick up at a later step and skip items [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. After any interruption, back up to the last item you are sure of.

callout.text: Many pilot errors happen when a pilot is off-frequency or heads-down, for example programming an FMS or GPS. Do high-workload jobs before you taxi [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(3) NOTE]].

check.q: When is the best time to load the GPS departure and check the autopilot preselects?
check.a: Before taxi or while stopped, so your eyes stay outside while moving [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(2)]] [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(4)]].

body.p: A planning trap: you brief one thing and ATC gives you another. Follow the clearance you actually receive, not the one you expected [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2) CAUTION]].

head: ATC change
What you do
rows: New runway
Rework performance, wind, abort point and emergency plan; re-brief [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]. Set the heading bug to the new runway [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]]
Intersection departure

You judge it. The reduced length and reduced declared distances must still cover your takeoff need. Ask for full length or for the distance if you want it [[33:252|AIM 4-3-10a]] [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10b]]
"Shortened" in the clearance
Construction has cut the runway; ATC won't say "full length" while it lasts [[1:369|PHAK 14-35]]
You can't comply safely
Say "UNABLE" right away [[1:367|PHAK 14-33]]

body.p: Before you enter any runway, be sure you are cleared. Scan the full length of the runway and the final approach. If anything is unclear, stop and ask ATC [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(4)]]. At any airport, scan the approach areas for landing traffic before you taxi onto the runway [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15a]]. At a nontowered airport, announce your intentions on the CTAF [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].
Close-together thresholds cause wrong-runway departures. Set the heading bug to your runway, align with it, and make one last instrument scan before adding power [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

bullets: "Line up and wait" is not a takeoff clearance [[1:368|PHAK 14-34]].
No takeoff clearance within 90 seconds of LUAW? Contact ATC [[1:369|PHAK 14-35]].
Entering the runway: all exterior lights on except landing lights. Landing lights on when cleared for takeoff [[7:10|AC 91-73B 7h(2)(d)]] [[7:10|AC 91-73B 7h(2)(f)]].
Read back takeoff clearances with your call sign and the runway [[7:8|AC 91-73B 7f(6)]].

check.q: "Runway 18 at Charlie 3, line up and wait." Two minutes pass with no call. What now?
check.a: Contact ATC. If no takeoff clearance comes within 90 seconds of LUAW, call them [[1:369|PHAK 14-35]] [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(9)]].

body.p: Every aircraft making lift trails two counter-rotating vortices [[34:147|AIM 7-4-1]]. They are strongest when the aircraft is heavy, clean and slow [[34:147|AIM 7-4-3]]. The usual danger is a roll your ailerons can't stop, and short-wingspan airplanes have it hardest [[34:148|AIM 7-4-3b]].

Vortices start when the aircraft rotates, so note the rotation point of the aircraft ahead. They sink several hundred feet per minute. Within 100 to 200 feet of the ground they spread sideways at 2 or 3 knots [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]].

A crosswind slows the upwind vortex and speeds up the downwind one. A light 1 to 5 knot crosswind can leave the upwind vortex sitting on the runway. A light quartering tailwind needs maximum caution [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4b]].

head: Situation
What to do
rows: Departing behind a larger aircraft
Rotate before its rotation point, climb above its path until you turn clear, avoid headings that cross below and behind it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b6]]
After a larger aircraft's low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go
Wait at least 2 minutes [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b8]]
Small airplane at an intersection behind a large (not heavy, not B757) on the same runway
ATC holds you 3 minutes ("Hold for wake turbulence"); you may request a waiver. Not required if within 500 feet of its start point, same direction [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10f]] [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10g]]
Intersection departure behind a heavy, or small behind a B757
3 minutes is mandatory; 4 minutes behind a super [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10h]]

callout.text: Warning or not, the pilot is expected to adjust operations and flight path to avoid serious wake encounters [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6a]].

check.q: A light 3-knot crosswind blows across the runway after a jet departs. Which vortex worries you most?
check.a: The upwind vortex. The crosswind cancels its sideways drift, so it can stay over the runway [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4b]].

bullets: Not reviewing the AFM/POH performance charts before takeoff [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].
Not clearing the area before taxiing onto the active runway [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].
Not checking engine instruments after applying takeoff power [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].
Moving the controls only part of the way [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].
Skipping the prop cycle, then an overspeed on takeoff [[24:239|AFH 12-8]].
Watching rpm instead of MP for carb ice with a constant-speed prop [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].
Programming avionics while rolling [[7:6|AC 91-73B 7d(3) NOTE]].
A rushed run-up, then IMC with gyros not up to speed [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].
Taking the runway change without re-briefing [[24:59|AFH 2-22]] [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2) CAUTION]].

callout.text: If a reading is outside POH limits, the check just did its job. Taxi back.

check.q: Name two errors the AFH lists that happen before the takeoff roll starts.
check.a: Not reviewing the performance charts, and not clearing the area before taxiing onto the runway [[24:138|AFH 6-6]].

f1.caption: Figure 7-9. Engine power output is indicated on the manifold pressure gauge.
f1.alt: Manifold pressure gauge marked IN Hg, scale 10 to 50, green arc from about 15 to just below 30, short red radial line just below 30, needle near 23.

f2.caption: Figure 7-35. Ammeter and loadmeter.
f2.alt: Left: round ammeter with zero at top center, -30 and -60 to the left, +30 and +60 to the right, needle at zero. Right: rectangular ALT AMPS loadmeter scaled 0, 30, 60 with the needle near 30.

f3.caption: Figure 2-6. Ground-based inspections include verification that “Xs” on the instrument display are displayed until the sensor activates.
f3.alt: Glass primary flight display with red Xs over the airspeed, altitude and vertical speed tapes, ATTITUDE FAIL across the attitude area, NAV and COM fields and transponder crossed out, while the heading bug 220, course 212, altimeter setting 29.92 and a GPS flight plan are shown.

f4.caption: Figure 14-49. Confusing runway/runway intersection.
f4.alt: Overhead drawing: a taxiway with a yellow centerline leads from an airplane up to the threshold of Runway 36, with yellow chevrons, white threshold stripes and the number 36. A second runway with a white dashed centerline runs diagonally right past the same spot.

f5.caption: FIG 7-4-6 Vortex Movement Near Ground - with Cross Winds
f5.alt: Jet seen from behind with two vortices sinking to the ground. With a 3-knot wind from the right, the left (downwind) vortex moves away at 6 knots (3 + 3) and the right (upwind) vortex stays nearly in place at 0 (3 - 3).

f6.caption: Figure 18-5. Turning back to the runway after engine failure.
f6.alt: Airplane loses its engine at 300 feet AGL after takeoff, turns back through 180 degrees and then to 225 degrees total, and ends up 1,016 feet below runway level, about 4,480 feet to the side.

scenario.title: Hot afternoon in a complex single
scenario.setup: You are training for your commercial in a complex single with a carbureted engine and a constant-speed prop. The towered airport sits at 4,500 feet and it is 30 °C. A friend rides in back. A large business jet (not heavy) just made a touch-and-go on Runway 33. Partway through your run-up, Ground calls you with a question. When you call ready, Tower says: "Runway 33 at Delta, intersection departure, line up and wait." You briefed a full-length departure.

questions.q: At run-up power the engine runs a little rough with the mixture full rich. What is likely, and what do you do?
questions.a: At high-elevation airports a rich mixture can foul the plugs during the run-up [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]]. Lean the way the POH says; one POH leans for maximum rpm in a full-throttle static run-up above 3,000 feet [[1:278|PHAK Figure 11-24]].

questions.q: Ground's call came halfway through the checklist. How do you pick it back up?
questions.a: Interruptions make you restart at a later step and skip items [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. Back up to the last item you are sure of. Keep looking outside in case the brakes slip at run-up power [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

Only if the reduced runway and reduced declared distances still cover your POH takeoff distance for 4,500 feet and 30 °C [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10b]]. Ask Tower for the distance; it is given rounded down to the nearest 50 feet [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10c]]. If it isn't enough, ask for full length or say "unable" [[33:252|AIM 4-3-10a]] [[1:367|PHAK 14-33]].
Its vortices settle and drift along the runway. Wait at least 2 minutes before your takeoff, especially in a light quartering wind [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b8]].

questions.q: How does today change your engine-failure plan?
questions.a: High density altitude means a longer roll and a weaker climb [[24:133|AFH 6-1]], so you reach any turn-back altitude later, if at all. Brief a real abort point and a straight-ahead landing area [[24:146|AFH 6-14]] [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

questions.q: Your friend wants to chat about the view during the line-up. What do you say?
questions.a: Ask for a sterile cockpit until you are clear of the terminal area, but to speak up about any traffic or conflict [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(b)]] [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7c]].

skills.do: Show the examiner today's POH takeoff distance for the weight, density altitude, wind and surface, compare it with the runway (or intersection) available, and name your abort point and VR, VX and VY.
skills.practice: Before every flight, work the chart and the accelerate-stop estimate (takeoff ground roll plus landing ground roll) out loud [[24:146|AFH 6-14]] [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]].

skills.do: Complete the AFM/POH before-takeoff checklist item by item, including the prop cycle and avionics setup, and give the takeoff briefing out loud.
skills.practice: Chair-fly the checklist and the sample briefing at home until you can explain each item's reason [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

skills.do: Stop on a firm, debris-free spot, clear of other aircraft and the taxiway, nose into the wind, nothing behind you, nosewheel straight.
skills.practice: On every run-up, tell your instructor why you chose the spot and what is behind the tail [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

skills.do: Look outside between checklist items, catch any creeping or traffic, and keep heads-down work for when you are stopped.
skills.practice: Use one item inside, one look outside; have your CFI interrupt you mid-check and practice backing up a step [[24:58|AFH 2-21]] [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

skills.do: Verify oil temperature and pressure, CHT, mags, carb heat if equipped, prop cycle, volts or ammeter, suction and avionics are within POH limits, and trim, flaps, fuel, prop and cowl flaps are set for takeoff; confirm full static rpm on the roll.
skills.practice: Say each reading against its POH limit as you check it, and call "rpm within 40 of red line, instruments green" on every takeoff roll [[24:239|AFH 12-8]] [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

quiz.q: Why do you move the prop control through a full cycle during the run-up?
options: To clear carbon from the spark plugs
To test each magneto on its own
To check the system and circulate warm oil through the governor
To cool the cylinders before takeoff
quiz.why: Cycling the prop proves the system works and circulates fresh warm oil through the governor; skipping it can lead to an overspeed on takeoff [[24:239|AFH 12-8]].

quiz.q: A FADEC-equipped piston airplane does away with which controls?
options: Magnetos, carb heat and a mixture lever
A throttle lever
An oil pressure gauge
A propeller
quiz.why: FADEC eliminates magnetos, carburetor heat, mixture controls and priming; a single throttle lever is typical [[1:180|PHAK 7-20]].

quiz.q: At the run-up the ammeter needle sits on the minus side. What does that mean?
options: The battery is charging normally
The voltage regulator has failed
More current is leaving the battery than is being replaced
The loadmeter is reading zero
quiz.why: A minus indication means more current is being drawn from the battery than is being replaced. Full-scale minus means an alternator problem [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]].

quiz.q: You ask Tower how much runway is left from an intersection. How is the distance given?
options: Rounded up to the nearest 100 feet
Exact to the foot
As the full set of declared distances
Rounded down to the nearest 50 feet
quiz.why: Controllers give the measured distance rounded down to the nearest 50 feet, and can't give declared distances from the intersection [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10c]].

options: Enter the runway and hold for a takeoff clearance
Take off once the runway looks clear
Hold short of the runway
Back-taxi for a full-length departure
quiz.why: LUAW is not a takeoff clearance. It is only a clearance to enter the runway and hold in position [[1:368|PHAK 14-34]].

quiz.q: Near the ground, how fast do a larger aircraft's vortices spread sideways in no wind?
options: About 10 to 15 knots
They don't move
About 2 or 3 knots
At the jet's taxi speed
quiz.why: Within 100 to 200 feet of the ground, vortices move laterally at 2 or 3 knots [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4a4]].

quiz.q: You reach your planned lift-off point and are not yet airborne. What should you do?
options: Pull back hard to force lift-off
Add flaps to help it fly
Keep going; most airplanes lift off late
Discontinue the takeoff right away
quiz.why: If that point is reached and you are not airborne, take immediate action to discontinue the takeoff [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

quiz.q: Entering the departure runway before takeoff clearance, which lights does AC 91-73B suggest?
options: All exterior lights off to avoid glare
All exterior lights on except the landing lights
Only the landing light
Only the taxi light
quiz.why: Turn on all lights except landing lights when entering the runway; landing lights go on when you are cleared for takeoff [[7:10|AC 91-73B 7h(2)(d)]] [[7:10|AC 91-73B 7h(2)(f)]].

quiz.q: At a high-elevation airport, a full-rich mixture during the run-up can cause:
options: Carburetor ice
Spark plug fouling and roughness
Prop overspeed
A high suction reading
quiz.why: A too-rich mixture at high elevation can foul the plugs during the run-up, so lean per the AFM/POH [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]].

quiz.q: Which is part of the avionics setup in the before-takeoff check?
options: Oil quantity and filler cap
Tire pressure and brake wear
Frequencies, nav source and course, autopilot preselects, transponder
Fuel sump samples
quiz.why: Avionics are set with frequencies, initial navigation sources and courses, autopilot preselects and transponder codes [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

takeaways: Use the AFM/POH checklist and be able to say why, what failure looks like, and the limit for each item.
Run up on a firm, clear spot, into the wind, with nothing behind the prop blast.
Constant-speed prop: cycle it at about 1,600 rpm; on the roll, rpm within 40 of red line.
Carb ice with a constant-speed prop shows on manifold pressure, not rpm.
Program avionics and run checklists while stopped; one item inside, one look outside.
New runway or intersection: recheck length, wind and wake, then re-brief out loud.
Brief the abort point and engine-failure plan; straight ahead is usually safest.
cfi_notes: Examiners probe K1a and K1b: for each item, ask 'why?' and 'what would a failure look like?' Accept POH numbers, not guesses.
Students moving up from fixed-pitch trainers often look for carb ice on the tach. Make them call MP during the carb heat check [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].
Interrupt the student mid-checklist with a radio call and see whether they back up or skip ahead [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].
Give a surprise runway change or intersection at the hold short line and require a full re-brief with new numbers [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10b]].
Have the student state a turn-back altitude for your airplane only after you have demonstrated it at altitude; AFH 18-7 warns against untrained turn-backs [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].
AFH 2-21 mentions feathering props and FADEC dual-ignition checks; keep the lesson single-engine and teach the AFM/POH test for the airplane you fly.
AFH Figure 18-5 shows 4,480 feet to the side while the AFH 18-7 text says 4,200 feet; quote the text, or avoid the number.

The autopilot check wording comes from AFH 13-8 (multiengine chapter) and the electric trim check and trim-runaway wording from AFH 17-10 and 17-14 (light-sport chapter). The lesson uses only their general points; teach the actual tests from the avionics AFM/POH supplement.
gaps: Run-up rpm, allowable mag drop, prop cycle rpm and count, oil and CHT limits, VR, VX, VY and best glide are airplane-specific and come from the AFM/POH, not these sources.
Autopilot and electric trim ground tests are only described in general terms (AFH 13-8, AFH 17-10, AFH 17-14, PHAK 6-12); the actual steps are in the avionics AFM/POH supplement.
The only source wording for autopilot preflight checks (AFH 13-8) sits in the multiengine chapter; the lesson uses only its general, single-engine-applicable points.
Fuel-injected engines' alternate air check is not described in the sources beyond PHAK 7-7; teach it from the POH.
The sources say little about FOD at piston run-ups beyond AFH 2-21; PHAK 7-23 defines FOD for turbine engines only.

activities.title: Run-up readings: go or no-go?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Left mag drops 75 rpm; POH allows 150
Engine quits when switched to LEFT
No rpm drop on either magneto
Constant-speed prop, carb heat on: MP drops and holds steady
Prop cycle: rpm drops smoothly, then comes back
Oil pressure below the minimum red line
Suction 5.0 "Hg at 2,000 rpm; POH says 4.8 to 5.2

activities.why: Mag limits and no-drop [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]] [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]; carb heat [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]; prop cycle [[24:239|AFH 12-8]]; ammeter [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]; oil pressure [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]; suction [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

activities.title: Cycle the constant-speed prop
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Start and warm up with the prop control full forward (low pitch, high rpm)
Set manifold pressure for about 1,600 rpm
Move the prop control slowly to high pitch, low rpm
Move the prop control back to the low pitch takeoff position

activities.title: What does a good check look like?
activities.intro: Tap an item, then tap what you check for.

pairs.l: Red Xs on a glass display
pairs.r: Clear as each sensor comes on line
Self-test and trim checks before you engage it
Full, free and correct in all directions

activities.title: Work the takeoff numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: POH takeoff ground roll is 1,400 feet and landing ground roll is 900 feet. Estimated runway needed to accelerate to takeoff speed and then stop, in feet?
items.why: Add the two ground rolls: 1,400 + 900 = 2,300 ft [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

items.q: Zero-wind takeoff distance is 1,600 feet. The headwind is 50 percent of your takeoff speed. About how far, in feet?
items.why: A headwind of 50 percent of takeoff speed gives about 25 percent of the zero-wind distance: 1,600 x 0.25 = 400 ft [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]].

items.q: Takeoff distance is 1,500 feet at your planned weight. You load 10 percent more weight. At least how far, in feet?
items.why: 10 percent more weight means at least 21 percent more distance: 1,500 x 1.21 = 1,815 ft [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]].

items.q: Like the FAA example, but the engine quits at 500 feet AGL: 4-second reaction, then a standard-rate turn (3 degrees per second) through 225 degrees, descending 1,000 fpm. How many feet below runway elevation do you end up?
items.why: 225 / 3 = 75 s, plus the 4 s reaction = 79 s. 79 / 60 x 1,000 fpm = 1,316 ft lost, the same loss as the FAA example (it does not depend on the failure altitude). 1,316 - 500 = 816 ft below the runway [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

activities.title: True or false: eyes and attention
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Running the before-takeoff checklist while taxiing through complex intersections is fine if you go slowly.
cards.why: No. Do pre-departure checklists only when stopped or taxiing straight ahead with no complex intersections [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(a)]].

cards.s: Load the GPS departure before taxi or while stopped.
cards.why: Yes. Enter navigation data before taxi, and do heads-down tasks while stopped so you keep watching outside [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(2)]] [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(4)]].

cards.s: A sterile cockpit means passengers should never speak, even about a conflict.
cards.why: No. Remind everyone about the sterile cockpit, but encourage them to speak up if they see a potential conflict [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(b)]].

cards.s: Phones may stay on during taxi as long as they are on silent.
cards.why: No. Phone use is discouraged during taxi; make sure everyone turns phones and devices off [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(j)]].

cards.s: At run-up power, a slipping brake can let the airplane roll forward unnoticed if you only look inside.
cards.why: Yes. That is why you split attention, one item inside, one look outside [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

cards.s: Mechanical gyros are ready the moment the engine starts, so a quick run-up before IMC is fine.
cards.why: No. Gyros need time to spool up; a hasty run-up and departure into IMC is unadvisable [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

activities.title: Am I on the right runway?
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.
activities.why: PHAK says Figure 14-49 shows a taxiway leading to multiple runways, the kind of spot that causes wrong-runway departures [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]]. Runways have white, segmented centerlines; taxiways have continuous yellow centerlines [[7:9|AC 91-73B 7g(5)]], so the white dashed strip is the other runway. Designators and threshold markings [[33:139|AIM 2-3-3b]] [[33:140|AIM 2-3-3h]].

activities.title: Departure day in N731CP
activities.intro: You are flying N731CP, a complex single with a carbureted engine and a constant-speed prop, from a towered airport on a cool morning with one passenger. A regional jet is departing ahead of you. Decide each step.

steps.s: Mid run-up your passenger starts asking about the scenery.
options: Chat and keep working the checklist
Ask for a sterile cockpit, but to speak up about traffic
Skip the rest of the checklist to save time
Taxi to the runway and finish there
steps.why: Ask passengers to avoid unnecessary talk during taxi and departure, but encourage them to report conflicts [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(b)]] [[7:5|AC 91-73B 7c]].

steps.s: Carb heat ON: manifold pressure drops, then slowly rises.
options: Normal; no ice was there
Ice was there and is melting; keep heat on until it clears
The governor failed; shut down
Ignore it; rpm did not change
steps.why: With a constant-speed prop, an MP drop followed by a gradual rise means ice was present. Leave the heat on until all ice is gone [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

steps.s: Tower: "N731CP, Runway 9 at Bravo, intersection departure, line up and wait." You planned full length.
options: Line up; ATC checks the length
Hold short, ask the distance from Bravo, rework performance and re-brief
Ask for an immediate takeoff instead
Line up first, then do the math
steps.why: You must judge whether the intersection is long enough and tell ATC if you want full length or the distance [[33:252|AIM 4-3-10a]] [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10b]]. Re-brief for the new plan [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

steps.s: The numbers work and you accept Bravo. Tower adds: "Hold for wake turbulence." The jet took off from the runway end.
options: Request a waiver right away; small airplanes don't need spacing
Wait the 3 minutes while its vortices sink and drift
Go now and turn below the jet's climb path
Ask to cancel and taxi back
steps.why: ATC holds a small airplane 3 minutes at an intersection behind a large aircraft on the same runway; a waiver means you accept the wake risk [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10f]]. Vortices sink and linger near the runway [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]].

steps.s: You are lined up and waiting. 90 seconds go by with no word.
options: Keep waiting quietly
Contact Tower
Take off; LUAW means you are next
Taxi off the runway without calling
steps.why: If a takeoff clearance doesn't come within 90 seconds of LUAW, contact ATC [[1:369|PHAK 14-35]].

steps.s: Cleared for takeoff. At full power the tach holds 200 rpm below red line.
options: Continue; it will come up with speed
Reject: throttle idle, brake, keep straight
Pull the prop control back a little
Rotate early to get airborne
steps.why: A constant-speed prop should give within 40 rpm of red line as soon as full power is set [[24:239|AFH 12-8]]. A malfunctioning powerplant is a reason to reject: idle, maximum braking, directional control [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

final_quiz.q: Constant-speed prop, red line 2,700 rpm. At full power on the takeoff roll the tach reads 2,640. What is the AFH guidance?
options: Normal; anything within 100 rpm is fine
Normal; rpm builds with airspeed
It is 60 rpm low, more than 40; treat it as a malfunction
Pull the prop control back slightly
final_quiz.why: The tach should come up to within 40 rpm of red line as soon as full power is applied [[24:239|AFH 12-8]]. 2,700 - 2,640 = 60 rpm, so reject for a powerplant problem [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

final_quiz.q: Before start at a sea-level airport on a standard day, what does the manifold pressure gauge read?
options: About 29.92 "Hg
About 12 "Hg
Zero
At the red line
final_quiz.why: With the engine not running, the MP gauge shows ambient air pressure, for example 29.92 "Hg; at idle it drops to about 12 "Hg [[1:166|PHAK 7-6]].

final_quiz.q: The right mag drop is well over the POH limit and the engine runs rough on it. What are likely causes?
options: Low fuel and a clogged vent
Carb ice and a rich mixture
A weak vacuum pump
Fouled plugs, broken or shorted wires, or bad timing
final_quiz.why: Don't fly until it is fixed. Causes include fouled plugs, broken or shorted wires, or improperly timed firing [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]] [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]].

final_quiz.q: Zero-wind takeoff distance is 2,000 feet. You have a headwind that is 10 percent of your takeoff speed. About how far?
options: About 1,800 feet
About 2,420 feet
About 1,620 feet
About 1,000 feet
final_quiz.why: A headwind of 10 percent of takeoff speed cuts distance about 19 percent: 2,000 x 0.81 = 1,620 ft [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]].

final_quiz.q: All electrical equipment is off. What does the loadmeter show?
options: Only the current the battery needs to charge
Always zero
Full scale
Alternator voltage
final_quiz.why: A loadmeter shows the load on the alternator; with everything off it shows only the battery's charging current [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]].

final_quiz.q: You are in a small airplane at an intersection 400 feet from where a large jet began its takeoff, same direction. Must ATC give you the 3-minute wake interval?
options: Yes, always behind a large aircraft
No, it is not required within 500 feet, same direction
Only at night
Only if you request it
final_quiz.why: The 3-minute interval is not required when the intersection is 500 feet or less from the departure point of the preceding aircraft, both going the same way [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10g]].

final_quiz.q: Look at the figure. A 3-knot crosswind blows from the right after a jet takes off. Where is the wake most likely to linger?
options: Downwind of the runway, moving at 6 knots
Over the runway, from the upwind vortex
High above the jet's climb path
Nowhere; vortices end at liftoff
final_quiz.why: The crosswind cancels the upwind vortex's own 3-knot drift, so it can stay in place while the downwind one moves away at 6 knots [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4b]].

final_quiz.q: A heavy jet departs ahead of you on the same runway. How do you plan your takeoff?
options: Lift off past its rotation point and stay low
Lift off at the same point and match its climb
Rotate before its rotation point and climb above its path
Turn right after liftoff to pass under its path
final_quiz.why: Note its rotation point, rotate before it, climb above its path until turning clear, and avoid headings that cross below and behind it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6b6]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the AFH say a turn back after engine failure needs more than a standard-rate turn?
options: A standard-rate turn takes too much time and distance
Standard-rate turns can't be flown without power
Steep turns lower the stall speed
ATC requires a steep turn
final_quiz.why: In the example the 4-second reaction plus a standard-rate turn through 225 degrees uses 79 seconds and leaves the airplane 1,016 feet below the runway; a shallow turn gives an unacceptable solution [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

final_quiz.q: During the run-up Tower switches you from Runway 27 to Runway 9. What changes in your briefing?
options: Nothing; it is the same strip of pavement
Only the heading bug
Only the frequency
Wind, takeoff distance, abort point and emergency landing areas
final_quiz.why: The briefing covers runway, wind, speeds and engine-failure actions, so a new runway means a new brief [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]. Emergency options depend on the departure path, wind and terrain [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

final_quiz.q: Tower says: "Runway 36 shortened, cleared for takeoff." What does "shortened" tell you?
options: Expect a shorter takeoff clearance
Construction has cut the runway length available
Use a short-field technique
The runway is closed
final_quiz.why: ATC adds "shortened" while construction reduces runway length, and won't say "full length" during that time. Recheck your takeoff distance [[1:369|PHAK 14-35]].

final_quiz.q: You taxied quickly and ran up in a hurry. The weather ahead is IMC. What is the concern?
options: The oil will be too hot
The mags will foul
The prop governor will lock
Mechanical gyros may not be up to speed and indicating properly
final_quiz.why: A hasty taxi and run-up may not let mechanical gyros spool up to read properly, and departing into IMC is unadvisable [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

final_quiz.q: Trees stand half a mile past the departure end. Which climb speed fits the initial climb?
options: VY, for the most altitude per minute
VX, for the most altitude per distance
Best glide
Cruise climb
final_quiz.why: VX gives the most altitude gain over a given horizontal distance and is used to clear obstacles such as trees after takeoff [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].
